title: Making peace
hookLine: Aaron's way, lived: help two people reconcile
tomorrow: exiles in an enemy city get a letter. what does it tell them?

cards: Two people at one lunch table who won't look at each other. You can hear it: forks a little too loud, a silence where the jokes used to be. You're friends with both.

A collection of teachings called Avot de-Rabbi Natan says Aaron, the brother of Moses, had a way into exactly that silence. When two people quarreled, he went to each one alone. And what he said to each was the same.

teach.h: HE'S ASHAMED. HE WANTS YOU BACK.
teach.b: He'd sit with the first and say: look at your friend. He's tearing at his heart, saying, how can I face him? I'm ashamed.
I'm the one who wronged him. Aaron would sit there until the anger left that heart.

teach.h: THEN THE SAME TO THE OTHER.
teach.b: Then he'd go to the other and say the same. And when the two met, the text says, they embraced and kissed.
Hillel turns this into a calling in Pirkei Avot: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing. Peace doesn't wait to be found; somebody chases it.
Did the other one really say those words? The text doesn't tell us. But here's the line to tell a friend tonight.

The Talmud says it's allowed to change a detail for the sake of peace, and it points to God doing it. When Sarah laughed that her husband was too old, God told Abraham only that Sarah had called herself old.
Aaron's way isn't lying about what matters. It's carrying the softest true thing across the room, and going first. The embrace belongs to them.
The walking back and forth belongs to whoever pursues peace.

how: Jewish teaching holds up Aaron as the model peacemaker; Pirkei Avot calls people to be his disciples, loving and pursuing peace, and the tradition allows small changes of detail for the sake of peace between people.

o: forgiving someone who never said sorry
staying neutral so nobody can blame you
helping two people who quarrel find their way back

p: be of the disciples of Aaron
chasing it, not waiting for it
a detail God left out for peace

s: Aaron got the two people in one room first, then talked
he went to each one alone first; the embrace came when they met.
Hillel says to love peace and pursue peace
be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.
the Talmud says you may never change a single detail, even for peace
it allows changing a detail for peace, and points to God and Sarah's laugh.

games.q: your two aunts haven't spoken since a fight over wedding seating. one tells you privately: i miss her, but she started it. what's Aaron's next move?
o: go to the other aunt and tell her, truly, that her sister misses her.
tell the first aunt she's right, so she feels supported.
wait it out; pursuing peace means not getting involved.
games.why: Aaron went to each side alone and carried the softest true thing across, until the two could meet and embrace.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, one for each person in a quarrel you know. With each slow breath, lift them a little closer, until the palms meet.
Hold them there, and think of one true, kind thing each of them might want the other to hear.

wordCard.voice: Making peace: Aaron's way, going to each side alone with the softest true thing, until two people can meet.

orig.note: Hebrew: a pursuer of peace; Hillel's words for the disciples of Aaron.

carryVoice: Something to keep: pursue peace. Somebody has to walk back and forth for it. Day done.

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 12 (Aaron goes to each of two who quarreled, says the other is ashamed and wants peace; they embrace when they meet)
Mishnah Avot 1:12 (Hillel: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace)
Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (it is permitted to alter a detail for the sake of peace; God reported Sarah's words without 'my lord being old')
Genesis 18:12-13 (Sarah laughs; God tells Abraham she said she was old)
